metadata.title: Factors Influencing Students’ Achievements in the Content and Cognitive Domains in TIMSS 4th Grade Science and Mathematics in the United Arab Emirates

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2015 grade 4 microdata for mathematics and science in the UAE and applies TIMSS’s complex survey weighting approach that accounts for the multistage sampling of schools, classrooms, and students. The authors state that they followed recommendations for calculating sampling weights that include student and class weight factors, and they use Jackknife Repeated Replication (JRR) to estimate sampling errors. Plausible values (PVs) are combined with the survey design using the IEA IDB Analyzer, and the merged dataset is then analyzed in Stata with survey commands that incorporate PVs, JRR, and sampling weights. The paper does not report a separate unweighted ML analysis; instead, it relies on TIMSS’s PV+survey-weight workflow for regression/SEM.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Secondary analysis of TIMSS 2015 for grade 4 students in the UAE, restricted to mathematics and science assessment items and student questionnaire indices. The analytic sample is the TIMSS grade 4 cohort in the UAE (558 schools: 372 private and 186 public; 21,177 students). The study performs data cleaning (e.g., recoding gender to 0/1, rescaling Likert responses such as “Never” and “Strongly Disagree” to 1) and applies listwise deletion for multivariate analyses, dropping cases with missing data rather than imputing.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Multiple linear regression (PV-based): R² = 0.12. Significant predictors: Breakfast on school days (b=2.52, p=0.01), Bullying (b=-13.10, p<0.001), Like learning mathematics (b=-5.13, p=0.033), Engaging teaching in mathematics lessons (b=11.5, p<0.001), Student confidence in mathematics (b=41.07, p<0.001). Gender not significant (b=-1.41, p=0.71).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2015 Grade 4 Mathematics (UAE) the study leveraged Breakfast on school days, Student bullying, Like learning mathematics, Engaging teaching in math, and Student confidence in math to predict mathematics achievement (Plausible Values), finding that student confidence and engaging teaching were strongly positive while bullying was strongly negative and liking mathematics was negative. This indicates that UAE grade 4 mathematics improvement efforts should prioritize strengthening students’ confidence and classroom engagement while implementing anti-bullying and carefully supporting students’ attitudes toward mathematics, though the study is correlational and not causal.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Multiple linear regression (PV-based): R² = 0.16. Significant predictors: Breakfast on school days (b=2.20, p=0.032), Bullying (b=-16.69, p<0.001), Like learning science (b=21.57, p<0.001), Student confidence in science (b=43.40, p<0.001). Engaging teaching in science lessons not significant (b=0.32, p=0.91). Gender not significant (b=2.83, p=0.50).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2015 Grade 4 Science (UAE) the study leveraged Breakfast on school days, Student bullying, Like learning science, Engaging teaching in science, and Student confidence in science to predict science achievement (Plausible Values), finding that student confidence and liking science were strongly positive while bullying was strongly negative; breakfast showed a smaller positive association. This indicates that UAE grade 4 science interventions should focus on building students’ confidence and science interest and reducing bullying, while recognizing that the measured engagement in science teaching was not a significant predictor in this model.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2015 Grade 4 Mathematics (UAE) — PV-based content/cognitive domains via SEM
main_findings.target_variable: Mathematics content domains (Number, Geometry, Data Display) — SEM latent outcomes
main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM fit (weak): SRMR = 0.42; CD = 0.30. Directional results across content domains: breakfast, engaging teaching in math, and student confidence in math had positive effects; bullying and liking learning mathematics had negative effects. Gender effects varied by domain (positive for Data Display and Geometry; negative for Number).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2015 Grade 4 Mathematics (UAE) the study leveraged breakfast on school days, student bullying, liking learning mathematics, engaging teaching in math lessons, student confidence in math, and gender to model mathematics content domains (Number, Geometry, Data Display) via SEM, finding that breakfast, engagement, and confidence were consistently positive while bullying and liking mathematics were negative. This indicates that curriculum-aligned classroom engagement and confidence-building strategies may be broadly beneficial across math content areas, but anti-bullying and attitude-support measures are needed because bullying and “liking math” showed adverse associations.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2015 Grade 4 Science (UAE) — PV-based content/cognitive domains via SEM
main_findings.target_variable: Science content domains (Life Science, Physics, Earth Science) — SEM latent outcomes
main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM fit (poor): SRMR = 0.40; CD = 0.39. Directional results: breakfast, liking learning science, and student confidence in science had positive effects; bullying had a negative effect across science content domains. Gender effects varied by domain (positive for Life Science; negative for Earth Science and Physics).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2015 Grade 4 Science (UAE) the study leveraged breakfast on school days, student bullying, liking learning science, engaging teaching in science lessons, student confidence in science, and gender to model science content domains (Life Science, Physics, Earth Science) via SEM, finding that breakfast, science interest, and confidence were positive while bullying was negative. This indicates that science achievement gains in the UAE may be supported by student well-being and confidence/interest-building, alongside targeted support for gender-differentiated performance patterns across specific science content areas.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses TIMSS 2015 grade 4 secondary data for the UAE (21,177 students; 558 schools) to examine how student factors relate to mathematics and science achievement in both content and cognitive domains. The authors analyze PV-based outcomes using TIMSS’s PV framework and Jackknife Repeated Replication (JRR) with sampling weights, and they handle missingness via listwise deletion. In multiple linear regression, mathematics achievement shows R² = 0.12, with student confidence in math (b=41.07) and engaging teaching in math (b=11.5) as strong positive predictors, while bullying (b=-13.10) is strongly negative. For science, R² = 0.16, with student confidence in science (b=43.40) and liking science (b=21.57) positive and bullying (b=-16.69) negative. SEM results indicate weak/poor model fit (SRMR around 0.40–0.43), and the study is correlational (no causal identification), so policy should be framed as associations rather than effects.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The paper does not train or evaluate machine learning algorithms (e.g., Random Forest, XGBoost, SVM). Instead, it uses PV-based multiple linear regression and Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) with survey-weighted TIMSS procedures. Therefore, ml_techniques is intentionally left empty and main_findings capture the regression/SEM predictive associations rather than ML model performance.
